Senses.Explanation: Prop up the broken earthenware basin: Shiqi Tongyun uses the phrase while patrons rebuild the Buddha hall and renew the ancestral seat; Daxiu Zhu uses it for new and old officeholders exerting themselves together. When Shiqi Tongyun inaugurates a rebuilt Buddha hall, he credits the patrons' strength with raising the long-neglected ancestral seat and “propping up the broken earthenware basin.” Daxiu Zhu makes the cooperation explicit: new and old officeholders must exert themselves together, while Baichi Xingyuan answers a question about building achievement with “everyone lend a hand” before urging the officers to support the basin together. Jieweizhou Xingzhou supplies the limit: even toppling a towering peak and propping up the broken basin remains adaptive teaching and is not yet remarkable in a patch-robed monk's own portion.

SearchAliases: the bottom drops out of the bucket
Senses.Explanation: A bucket loses its bottom in the middle of use: contents spill, the vessel no longer holds, and the event can be seen. Chan records reuse that concrete collapse as a comparison after a blow or a phrase, as a direct answer to ‘What is buddha?’, and as an image whose literal kitchen occurrence remains visible. Its comparison form 'like the bucket-bottom falls out' (如桶底脫) occurs 38 times, including 26 exact endings in 'resembling the bucket-bottom falling out' (桶底脫相似). Xuefeng reports that after Deshan struck him, 'at that time I was as if the bucket-bottom had fallen out' (我當時如桶底脫相似); Yantou immediately challenges what Xuefeng brought in through the gate. Yuanwu uses the same comparison after 'under one phrase' (一言之下) and elsewhere joins the literal image to 'the mechanisms are exhausted' (桶底脫機關盡). The phrase is also recorded as a direct answer: asked 'What is buddha?' (如何是佛), Shoushan Huaizhi says, 'the bucket-bottom falls out' (桶底脫). A separate kitchen encounter uses the words literally: while noodles are cooking, the bucket-bottom suddenly falls out, the assembly cries that it is a pity, and the cited speaker says, 'the bucket-bottom falling out should itself be cause for joy—why are you distressed?' (桶底脫自合歡喜), before agreeing that the lost bucket of noodles is regrettable. The physical event and its simile therefore share one graph-level sense while appearing in an answer, recollection, comment, and kitchen exchange.

Senses.Explanation: Right then and there: a temporal expression marking something as occurring without an intervening interval. Shanglan Shun's verse says accumulated ignorance disappears right then; the Five Lamps narrator says Zhitian awakens on the spot when shown the blowing-a-hair case. Huangbo Xiyun uses it for the time of becoming clear without retaining a mark of clarity, while Linji Yixuan uses it for being without further business after turning the light back and recognizing no difference from the patriarchs and buddhas. Huqiu Shaolong says that if listeners trust the presented mind-settling scene, the mind is settled right then. Wuyi Yuanlai attaches the expression to one thought not arising, Miyin to the ice-like disappearance of a raised repentance case, Xuedou Chongxian to a mirror distinguishing beautiful and ugly as soon as it is set up, and the Yongzheng Emperor to a selected saying and discriminating consciousness shattering on the spot. The Zen record prizes the compressed timing, but the word itself remains a temporal modifier: it does not by itself name a teaching, a prescribed exercise, or a distinct temporal entity.

Senses.Explanation: Meeting the occasion means answering or acting aptly at the live trigger-point of an encounter. The phrase can introduce a request—“with one phrase meeting the occasion, please speak the teaching” (一句當機請師說法)—or appraise an immediate response. Feiyin Tongrong strikes the staff and says, “freed through on the occasion; it is no other thing” (當機透脫，更非別物). Yuanwu's verse says that buddhas and patriarchs “value what is ready-made when meeting the occasion” (佛祖當機貴見成) and immediately calls for someone to come before the assembly and settle doubt. Thus the corpus bends a general word for apt timing toward the live occasion of encounter, question, answer, and response.

Senses.Explanation: One should observe the time and conditions directs attention to the occasion and the circumstances on which an event depends. Micang Kai uses the formula in a letter about undertakings within his house: conditions may reach fulfillment, while forcing an undertaking at the wrong time can exchange one injury for another. Weilin Daopei recites the familiar Buddha-nature formula in a New Year's address, then asks what time it is now and answers with the change from the old year's tail to the new year's head. The Five Lamps Compendium preserves the formula as an explicitly marked scriptural quotation in Baizhang Huaihai's explanation after Guishan Lingyou's awakening. These uses retain the literal work of 時節 and 因緣; the sources do not require a separate master-specific sense.

Senses.Explanation: Miss it face to face is a sharp encounter verdict: the requested matter is already present in the exchange, yet the questioner or audience passes it by at the very moment of meeting it. Jingshan Zhice answers the question why the Tiantai master is beneath his questioner's feet with the headword itself. Sanshan Denglai likewise gives it as the answer when a hypothetical interlocutor calls his reply worlds apart, while Yuanwu Keqin uses it as his answer for the Yunmen house. The phrase also warns an audience against losing the immediate event. Tianyin Yuanxiu says the monastery's timber, tiles, and stones are already turning the teaching wheel and tells the assembly not to miss it face to face; Liao'an Qingyu asks why half the audience still does so despite an overt explanation. In another Yuanwu address, even Yunmen and Muzhou are judged to have missed face to face, so the verdict is not reserved for novices.

Senses.Explanation: To miss something face-to-face is to fail to recognize what is directly present; speakers apply the warning to a person, ordinary sights, a staff, and an encounter before the assembly. The phrase occurs as a verdict, a warning, and an author's acknowledgment. Meixi Du pairs two kinds of people: those who stand out shoulder it directly, while those confused about the head and recognizing a shadow miss it face-to-face (超群拔萃的，直下荷擔；迷頭認影的，當面錯過). In a letter he says that on first meeting a correspondent he did not recognize the correspondent's freedom and literary quality, “truly what is called missing it face-to-face” (誠所謂當面錯過也); this is the corpus's only formula using “what is called” for the term. Boshan Wuyi says, after asking whether anyone can assess the value of what he has presented, “one still must not miss it face-to-face” (也不可當面錯過). Elsewhere Boshan lists “rice comes from grain, soup from water, and a nun is a woman,” then says “do not miss it face-to-face” (飯是米做底、湯是水做底、師姑是女人做底，切莫當面錯過). Yunxi's record places the warning after “kites fly and fish leap; mountains stand and water flows” (鳶飛魚躍，山峙水流，切莫當面錯過). Panlong calls on his staff to bring news to the assembly, warns them not to miss it face-to-face, raises the staff, and asks whether they understand. The exact phrase is attested.

Senses.Explanation: Tao Yuanming is the poet whom these records recognize through wine, chrysanthemums, and his decision to return home. Masters make that literary figure work in public speech: 'if it were Tao Yuanming, he would frown and go home' dismisses a labored formulation, while other addresses pair his return with withdrawal from a crowded or defiled scene. He is therefore a pre-Chan figure as deployed by Chan speakers, not a lineage master and not merely a biographical name.
